title: The Python's Contentment and the Ocean's Depth
story:
"The python taught me contentment," the avadhuta said. "He lies where he happens to be, and whatever comes within his reach — fine food or foul, much or little — he takes. If nothing comes, he lies still for days on end, without effort, without pursuit, without complaint. He does not hunt, he does not plan, he does not grieve the meal that passed him by; hunger comes and goes, and he is still the python either way. So the sage accepts what chance brings and does not run after more. He carries a body full of vigor and strength, yet he does not spend it on striving; his hands do what needs doing, but his acts leave no trace on him, because they are not born of desire."

The king, whose days were a long argument with appetite — the next campaign, the next pleasure, the next proof of his greatness — heard this and felt the strangest lightness, as if a knot had been loosened inside him.

"The ocean taught me depth," the avadhuta said. "The rivers pour into it, and it does not swell; the rivers dry up, and it does not sink. The rivers may rage in flood or fail in drought; the sea receives both without preference, because its depth is not borrowed from them. It stays deep, full, and serene — so deep that no one can fathom it, so still that no one can stir it. Whatever pours in, whatever is withheld, its fullness is its own. So the sage remains the same whether the world pours gifts upon him or leaves him empty-handed. Whether his desires are fulfilled or he is left destitute, he is fixed on Narayana alone; that is his fullness, and it does not rise or fall with fortune."

Yadu looked at the wanderer — at the man who owned nothing and had just described the ocean as if it lived inside him. And slowly he understood that the python's stillness and the ocean's depth were one teaching: freedom does not come from having enough; it comes from not needing anything. The sage is not the man who has everything — he is the man who is complete without anything, like the sea that no river can fill and no drought can empty.

A wind moved through the forest, and the avadhuta sat in the middle of it, unmoved, like his teachers. The king, who had come to the forest to escape his court for a day, found that he had wandered into a school greater than any he had built. And the sage, seeing that the lesson had landed, spoke again — of the moth, and of the flame it cannot resist.
reflection: The python and the ocean teach the same freedom at two scales: the python accepts what comes without striving, the ocean stays full whether rivers come or not — and the two together show that contentment is not a matter of how much one has but of where one's center is. The sage's fullness is fixed on Narayana, so fortune can neither add to it nor take from it.
next_story_tease: Then he told of the moth, which cannot resist the flame.
hero_scene: A great python lies coiled and still beneath a tree, swallowing a scrap that chance brought it, while beyond the forest a vast calm ocean stretches unruffled under the sky — and the avadhuta gestures toward both as the king watches.

the vast serene ocean, deep and unmoved
the avadhuta gesturing toward his two teachers
King Yadu listening, the knot of desire loosening in his face
rivers pouring into the sea and drying up, the sea unchanged
